podcast.body: Regarded by some music historians as the first ever punk rock record, this track was the B-side of a one-off seven-inch single released in the summer of 1974. The song was recorded accidentally after Smith and her collaborator Lenny Kaye finished early while recording a cover of Jimi Hendrix's "Hey Joe." It recounts Smith's experiences working in a doll factory. A thousand copies were pressed and distributed to independent bookstores and record sellers, selling out almost instantly, which helped launch Smith's career as a recording artist and icon on the New York punk rock scene. "No one, man or woman, was making music quite like this back then."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.body: This poem, recited by Patti Smith with her musician friends vamping in the background, was recorded as the B-side to "Hey Joe" in June 1974, due to leftover time and money. It was written about a dead-end job Smith once held and unexpectedly captured the attention of the New York avant-garde underground, with its 1000 copies quickly selling out. It is often considered a contender for the "first true punk record." "Because they had some time and money left after recording Hay Joe, someone suggested that Patty read a poem that she had written about a dead-end job that she once held. Her musician friends just vamped along in the background as she read this poem."
